# The Blyx handbook

Blyx 0.2.1 · Released language and toolchain

Start with a complete fn main(). Run your program in the playground or use blyxc check FILE followed by blyxc run FILE. For a native executable, use blyxc build FILE with Rust and a host linker installed.

[Learn Blyx](https://www.blyx-lang.space/learn) · [Playground](https://www.blyx-lang.space/play) · [Executable subset](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/blob/blyx-main/docs/executable-subset.md) · [Full handbook](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/llms-full.txt)

The release supports synchronous functions, recursion, control flow and numeric vectors. Native projects can import Git-pinned Blyx packages and read files or command-line arguments. See the [ecosystem](https://www.blyx-lang.space/packages) for published libraries. GPU kernels, async tasks and a general tensor runtime are under development.

## First steps

### [Your first Blyx program](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/first-program)

Start in the browser, make a prediction, then edit and run your first line of Blyx.

#### Start with a running file

A program is a set of instructions written as text. The editor below contains a complete file. Select Run program and read the Output pane. If Run on edit is selected, changes run automatically. You can reset the example at any time.

#### Read the greeting

The two lines beginning with // are notes for the reader. Execution begins at fn main(). The braces enclose the work that main performs. Inside them, println! writes the text between the double quotes and finishes the line. The semicolon ends that instruction.

#### Change one thing

Replace World inside the quoted greeting with your name. Leave the quotes, parentheses, exclamation mark and semicolon where they are. Run again and compare the two greetings. Changing the text changes what your reader sees.

#### Let the computer calculate

Add println!(6 * 7); on a new line inside the braces. Blyx evaluates the multiplication before printing 42. Put double quotes around 6 * 7 and you will see the characters instead. The difference between a value and text describing a value will recur throughout the course.

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Blyx Example 1: Hello World
// Official Domain: https://blyx-lang.space

fn main() {
    println!("Hello, World from Blyx!");
}
```

Expected output

```
Hello, World from Blyx!
```

#### Practice

Make the program print Hello, Blyx! on its first line and 42 on its second.

Hint

Keep both print calls inside main. Use quotes for the greeting and leave the multiplication unquoted.

Solution

Each println! adds one line. The arithmetic expression evaluates before the second call.

Find

```blyx
println!("Hello, World from Blyx!");
```

Replace with

```blyx
println!("Hello, Blyx!");
    println!(6 * 7);
```

Output after the change

```
Hello, Blyx!
42
```

### [Numbers and expressions](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/arithmetic)

Use a packing problem to learn whole numbers, decimals, operator order and integer division.

#### Turn a question into an expression

How many rows of five can you fill with 23 items? Give the two counts names with let. Since both values are integers, items / row yields the number of whole rows. The remainder operator, %, gives the three items still on the table.

#### Choose whole or fractional units

The literal 23 has type i64, a signed 64-bit integer. The literal 23.0 has type f64, a 64-bit floating-point number. The expression 23.0 / 5.0 yields 4.6. Use integer counts for indivisible objects and decimal operands on both sides when a fraction matters.

#### Group an expression

Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition and subtraction. Read 2 + 3 * 4 as 2 + (3 * 4), which gives 14. In the editor, parentheses make (2 + 3) happen first, giving 20.

#### Choose useful test cases

A full row, one fewer than a full row, and zero items each tell you something different about the result. With a nonzero row size, full_rows * row + leftover reconstructs the input. Integer division by zero and integer overflow produce execution errors.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let items = 23;
    let row = 5;
    println!(items / row);
    println!(items % row);
    println!(23.0 / 5.0);
    println!((2 + 3) * 4);
}
```

Expected output

```
4
3
4.6
20
```

#### Practice

Pack 24 items in rows of five. Predict both integer results before running.

Hint

The division and remainder use items. The separate decimal example uses literal values.

Solution

Four complete rows hold 20 items. Four items remain. The decimal expression and the grouped expression still use their original literals.

Find

```blyx
let items = 23;
```

Replace with

```blyx
let items = 24;
```

Output after the change

```
4
4
4.6
20
```

### [Text, comments and output](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/text-output)

Build a receipt one value at a time and learn how strings differ from variable names.

#### Name the pieces

A string literal encloses text in double quotes. Inside "Total: " the final space separates the label from the price. Outside quotes, label refers to the value introduced by let. Writing "label" would print those five letters.

#### Assemble a line

print!(label) writes the label and leaves the cursor on that line. println!(cost) writes the integer and ends the line. The last call starts a new line with Paid. To display several values together, use consecutive calls. These macros take zero or one expression.

#### Write a useful comment

A // comment continues to the end of its line. A comment such as // price is in whole credits records the unit that the number alone cannot express. Put the calculation in a binding if you want to print it twice.

#### Read output precisely

An extra space, a missing line break or putting the numeric expression inside quotes can change a report. First compare the lines and then compare characters within each line. This is the same approach you can use when testing a longer program.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let label = "Total: ";
    let cost = 3 * 7;
    print!(label);
    println!(cost);
    println!("Paid");
}
```

Expected output

```
Total: 21
Paid
```

#### Practice

Change the quantity from three to five and replace the final receipt line with Thanks.

Hint

Edit the expression that defines cost, then edit the last quoted string.

Solution

Five units at seven credits cost 35. print! keeps the label and total on the same line.

Find

```blyx
3 * 7
```

Replace with

```blyx
5 * 7
```

Find

```blyx
"Paid"
```

Replace with

```blyx
"Thanks"
```

Output after the change

```
Total: 35
Thanks
```

## Language essentials

### [Bindings, mutation and scope](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/bindings)

Trace a name through nested blocks and choose when a value should change.

#### Bind a name

let level = 3; evaluates the right-hand expression and gives its result a name. An immutable binding is a useful default for a quantity that should keep the same value. Declare let mut when later statements need to update that particular binding.

#### Follow a name into a block

At the opening brace the program enters a new scope. The inner let level = 8; creates a second binding. A read of level starts in the current scope, so the first print sees 8. Leaving the block removes the inner binding and the outer 3 is visible again.

#### Change an existing binding

An assignment starts with the name, as in level = 8;. The interpreter finds the nearest binding with that name. Assignment requires a mutable binding and a compatible value kind. If there is an inner declaration, updating it only changes the inner value.

#### Accumulate a result

For a mutable integer counter, count += 1 adds one to the current value. The same updates work for subtraction, multiplication, division and remainder through -=, *=, /= and %=. Start a sum at zero and a product at one so the initial value preserves the first term.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let level = 3;
    {
        let level = 8;
        println!(level);
    }
    println!(level);
}
```

Expected output

```
8
3
```

#### Practice

Make both print calls show 8 by updating the outer level inside the block.

Hint

Use mut for the outer declaration and remove let from the inner statement.

Solution

There is now one mutable binding. The assignment reaches it and the new value is still visible after the block.

Find

```blyx
let level = 3;
```

Replace with

```blyx
let mut level = 3;
```

Find

```blyx
let level = 8;
```

Replace with

```blyx
level = 8;
```

Output after the change

```
8
8
```

### [Booleans and decisions](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/decisions)

Classify temperatures, then test exactly what happens at the boundaries.

#### Ask a yes-or-no question

A comparison such as t < 0.0 produces true or false. An if condition requires a boolean. The band function first checks for a value below zero. Its early return immediately sends the string frozen back to the caller.

#### Partition the remaining inputs

After the first check, every remaining input in this example is zero or warmer. The final if expression chooses mild below 30 and hot otherwise. Because this expression supplies the function’s result, there is no semicolon after its closing brace.

#### Read the comparison signs

Use == to compare for equality and != to test inequality. Use < or > for strict limits and <= or >= to include the limit itself. To combine rules, && requires both sides, || requires at least one, and ! reverses a boolean. Short-circuit evaluation skips the right side once the answer is known.

#### Test the boundary

Two implementations can agree on -2 and 10 and still disagree at zero. A boundary test deliberately uses the threshold itself. Here 0.0 skips the frozen branch and 30.0 skips the mild branch.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn band(t: f64) -> str {
    if t < 0.0 { return "frozen"; }
    if t < 30.0 { "mild" } else { "hot" }
}

fn main() {
    println!(band(-2.0));
    println!(band(0.0));
    println!(band(30.0));
}
```

Expected output

```
frozen
mild
hot
```

#### Practice

Change the rule so exactly 30 is mild. Keep the boundary at zero as it is.

Hint

Look for the comparison in the final if expression.

Solution

Including equality sends 30.0 through the mild branch. The negative and zero cases take their original branches.

Find

```blyx
t < 30.0
```

Replace with

```blyx
t <= 30.0
```

Output after the change

```
frozen
mild
mild
```

### [Functions, parameters and results](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/functions)

Give a calculation a name, call it more than once, and use its return value in another expression.

#### Define the interface

Read fn total(price: i64, quantity: i64) -> i64 as a function named total taking two signed integers and returning one signed integer. A parameter names a value inside the function. An argument is the value supplied by a call.

#### Trace a call

In total(7, 3), price receives 7 and quantity receives 3. The function multiplies them, finishes, and the caller receives 21. The binding first keeps that result in main. The second call uses new arguments and its result is added to first.

#### Return from a block

A final expression without a semicolon supplies the result. You can also write return price * quantity; to exit explicitly. A semicolon discards a final expression’s value. Keep an explicit return type on functions that return values when compiling a native executable.

#### Keep calculation separate from output

total can serve a receipt, a test or a larger calculation because it returns its answer. main decides what to print. Parameters belong to each call. Declare a local mutable accumulator when you need a value to change inside the function.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn total(price: i64, quantity: i64) -> i64 {
    price * quantity
}

fn main() {
    let first = total(7, 3);
    println!(first);
    println!(total(4, 2) + first);
}
```

Expected output

```
21
29
```

#### Practice

Make the second order four units at four credits. Print the combined total for both orders.

Hint

Only the second call in main needs different arguments.

Solution

The first order is 21 and the second is 16. Their sum is 37.

Find

```blyx
total(4, 2)
```

Replace with

```blyx
total(4, 4)
```

Output after the change

```
21
37
```

### [While loops and the Euclidean algorithm](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/control-flow)

Trace changing state and explain why a loop finishes.

#### Name the repeated work

The greatest common divisor is the largest positive integer that divides both inputs exactly. For nonnegative inputs with at least one positive, dividing x by y leaves a remainder. A number divides both x and y exactly if and only if it divides y and that remainder.

#### Trace the state

A while loop checks its condition before executing the body. Each pass replaces (x, y) with (y, x % y). Save the remainder first because overwriting x earlier would lose one of the inputs.

| Before the pass | Remainder | After the pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 48, 18 | 12 | 18, 12 |
| 18, 12 | 6 | 12, 6 |
| 12, 6 | 0 | 6, 0 |

#### Explain termination

When y is positive, the new remainder is at least zero and strictly smaller than y. Eventually y reaches zero. The guard prevents taking a remainder with a zero divisor and the final x supplies the answer.

#### Start with a small test

If the second argument already equals zero, no iteration runs. Swapping positive inputs can add a first iteration, but the same common divisors survive. Tracing two small examples by hand is a quick way to find a mistaken update order.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn gcd(a: i64, b: i64) -> i64 {
    let mut x = a;
    let mut y = b;
    while y != 0 {
        let remainder = x % y;
        x = y;
        y = remainder;
    }
    x
}

fn main() {
    println!(gcd(48, 18));
}
```

Expected output

```
6
```

#### Practice

Use 35 and 15 as inputs. Predict each remainder and the final result.

Hint

Start with 35 % 15, then divide 15 by that remainder.

Solution

The remainders are 5 and 0, so the last positive divisor is 5.

Find

```blyx
gcd(48, 18)
```

Replace with

```blyx
gcd(35, 15)
```

Output after the change

```
5
```

### [Break, continue and loop values](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/loop-exits)

Find the first matching integer and carry it out of a loop.

#### Choose a stopping rule

while is convenient when the decision to repeat belongs at the top. Here the program must construct a candidate before it can decide whether to stop. A loop expression lets the test live beside the value that will become the answer.

#### Follow one iteration

The counter starts at 9. The first pass increments it to 10. Its remainder on division by four is nonzero, so continue jumps back to the beginning. The update occurs before continue so the candidate moves forward on every pass.

#### Return a value from a loop

At 12 the condition for continue is false. break n exits the nearest loop and supplies 12 to the binding found. The semicolon after the loop expression completes the enclosing let declaration. An ordinary break also exits a while loop, without carrying a value.

#### Distinguish the destinations

continue returns to the next iteration, break leaves the current loop, and return leaves the current function. If your program stops with a step-budget error, trace the path through continue and check that the variable in the condition actually changes.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let mut n = 9;
    let found = loop {
        n += 1;
        if n % 4 != 0 { continue; }
        break n;
    };
    println!(found);
}
```

Expected output

```
12
```

#### Practice

Find the first multiple of five strictly greater than nine.

Hint

Keep the starting number and change the divisor.

Solution

The first candidate is 10. Its remainder on division by five is zero, so it becomes the loop result.

Find

```blyx
n % 4
```

Replace with

```blyx
n % 5
```

Output after the change

```
10
```

### [Recursion and the cost of a call](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/recursion)

Trace Fibonacci by hand, identify the base case, and decide when iteration is cheaper.

#### Specify a base case

In this example Fibonacci is defined on nonnegative integers with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1. Each call first checks whether its argument is smaller than two. A base case gives a direct answer and prevents another call.

#### Expand one call

For n = 4 the two subproblems are F(3) and F(2). F(3) needs F(2) and F(1), while each F(2) needs F(1) and F(0). Work back up the tree to get 2 + 1 = 3. Each invocation has its own parameter value.

#### Count work as well as depth

F(2) is evaluated twice in that small tree. Repeated subproblems make this recursive implementation expensive as n grows. An iterative version can carry the two most recent values in mutable bindings and advance one position per pass.

#### Choose a safe input

The interpreter has both a step budget and a maximum of 64 simultaneous calls. Keep practice inputs small. A native build also uses finite machine resources. Large Fibonacci numbers eventually exceed the checked i64 range regardless of the algorithm.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn fibonacci(n: i64) -> i64 {
    if n < 2 { return n; }
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);
}

fn main() {
    println!("Fibonacci(10):");
    println!(fibonacci(10));
}
```

Expected output

```
Fibonacci(10):
55
```

#### Practice

Print Fibonacci at position seven, with a matching label.

Hint

The function name also occurs in the label. Edit the label and the call.

Solution

Building the sequence from zero gives 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Position seven is 13.

Find

```blyx
"Fibonacci(10):"
```

Replace with

```blyx
"Fibonacci(7):"
```

Find

```blyx
fibonacci(10)
```

Replace with

```blyx
fibonacci(7)
```

Output after the change

```
Fibonacci(7):
13
```

## Numerical programming

### [Vectors and reductions](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/vectors)

Represent several readings in one value and combine them into a weighted mean.

#### Choose a representation

A vector literal such as [5.0, 7.0, 9.0] holds numeric elements in order. Element storage is f64, including when the literal contains whole numbers. A vector can be empty. Bind it to a name or pass it to a function whose parameter type is vector.

#### Read by position

Indices begin at zero. For these three readings, len(readings) is 3 and at(readings, 2) is 9. Use an integer index and keep it below the length. The release supports reading vector elements. Build an accumulator when you need to calculate a derived result.

#### Give one reading extra weight

A dot product multiplies pairs at matching positions and adds them. With weights [1.0, 1.0, 2.0], the weighted total is 5 + 7 + 18 = 30. The total weight is 4. Dividing produces 7.5, which is closer to the final reading than the ordinary mean.

#### State the input contract

dot requires equal vector lengths. For a weighted average with nonnegative weights, require a positive total weight. An empty pair can have a valid dot product of zero while its mean has a zero denominator. Decide how your program should handle that case before you divide.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let readings = [5.0, 7.0, 9.0];
    let weights = [1.0, 1.0, 2.0];
    println!(dot(readings, weights) / sum(weights));
}
```

Expected output

```
7.5
```

#### Practice

Give the first reading double weight and give each of the others weight one.

Hint

Keep the number of weights equal to the number of readings.

Solution

The weighted total becomes 10 + 7 + 9 = 26. Divide by four to get 6.5.

Find

```blyx
[1.0, 1.0, 2.0]
```

Replace with

```blyx
[2.0, 1.0, 1.0]
```

Output after the change

```
6.5
```

### [Scan a vector for its maximum](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/vector-scans)

Design a loop that finds the largest value even when every reading is negative.

#### Define the input

Finding a maximum requires at least one reading. This example supplies a nonempty literal. A reusable function should check len(readings) before indexing, or document and enforce the nonempty requirement at its call site.

#### Choose a starting value

Initialize peak from the first reading and begin the loop at index 1. Starting at zero as a candidate maximum would report a nonexistent zero for an all-negative input. The first real reading is a candidate you know belongs to the data.

#### Maintain a fact after every pass

Before reading index i, peak is the largest of the first i elements. Compare the next reading with peak, keep the larger value and increment i. The same fact now covers one more element. When i equals len(readings), the fact covers the whole input.

#### Estimate the cost

For n nonempty readings this scan performs n − 1 comparisons and stores a fixed number of local values beyond the input. A one-element vector skips the loop and returns its only element. Equal maxima do not change the reported value.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let readings = [-8.0, -1.0, -3.0];
    let mut peak = at(readings, 0);
    let mut i = 1;
    while i < len(readings) {
        let reading = at(readings, i);
        if reading > peak { peak = reading; }
        i += 1;
    }
    println!(peak);
}
```

Expected output

```
-1
```

#### Practice

Try a vector containing just -12.0. Decide whether the loop body will run.

Hint

After initialization the index and the vector length both equal one.

Solution

The condition is false before the first pass. The initial reading is already the maximum.

Find

```blyx
[-8.0, -1.0, -3.0]
```

Replace with

```blyx
[-12.0]
```

Output after the change

```
-12
```

### [Smooth a sequence with one running value](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/smoothing)

Turn a noisy signal into a sequence of estimates and trace how much history each estimate retains.

#### Set the initial state

The first reading is the first estimate. Print it before the loop and begin processing at index one. This convention gives one output per input, including for a single reading. The example assumes a nonempty signal because it reads index zero.

#### Blend old and new

Each later estimate is half the new reading plus half the previous estimate. For readings 10, 14, 18, the second estimate is 0.5 × 14 + 0.5 × 10 = 12. The third uses 12 as its old state and becomes 15.

#### Understand the tradeoff

More weight on the new reading makes the output respond faster to changes. Less weight preserves more history. Choose complementary weights that sum to one so a constant signal stays constant. A weight of one on the new reading reproduces the input.

#### Check a boundary case

Feed the algorithm three copies of 6. Its estimate should remain 6 after every pass. This checks both the initial value and the blend. Then change one input at a time so the reason for any output change is visible.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let signal = [10.0, 14.0, 18.0];
    let mut estimate = at(signal, 0);
    println!(estimate);
    let mut i = 1;
    while i < len(signal) {
        estimate = 0.5 * at(signal, i) + 0.5 * estimate;
        println!(estimate);
        i += 1;
    }
}
```

Expected output

```
10
12
15
```

#### Practice

Give the new reading weight 0.75 and the previous estimate weight 0.25.

Hint

Both coefficients occur on the line that updates estimate.

Solution

The second estimate is 13. The last uses 13 as its old state, yielding 16.75.

Find

```blyx
0.5 * at(signal, i) + 0.5 * estimate
```

Replace with

```blyx
0.75 * at(signal, i) + 0.25 * estimate
```

Output after the change

```
10
13
16.75
```

### [Fit a line and predict a value](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/numerical-models)

Fit a one-parameter model, inspect its assumptions, and predict the response at an unseen input.

#### Choose a model

Suppose measurements are proportional to their input and a zero input should produce a zero response. Use y = slope × x. This choice fixes the intercept at zero. Pair each input with its observed target by position in two equal-length vectors.

#### Find the slope

The least-squares slope through the origin is dot(samples, targets) / dot(samples, samples). The numerator adds input × observed response across the pairs. The denominator adds the squared inputs. It is positive when at least one input is nonzero.

#### Work a fit by hand

With x = [1, 2, 3, 4] and y = [2, 4, 6, 8], the numerator is 60 and the denominator is 30. The slope is 2. A new input of 5 yields 10. The fit function only returns a coefficient. main chooses where to predict.

#### Interpret a changed observation

Increase the last target by 3. The numerator increases by 4 × 3 while the denominator stays 30. The new slope is 72 / 30 = 2.4. One observation can move every future prediction because the fitted slope is shared.

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Fit y = slope * x by least squares through the origin.
fn fit(samples: vector, targets: vector) -> f64 {
    dot(samples, targets) / dot(samples, samples)
}

fn main() {
    let samples = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0];
    let targets = [2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0];
    let slope = fit(samples, targets);
    println!(slope);
    println!(slope * 5.0);
}
```

Expected output

```
2
10
```

#### Practice

Leave the training data unchanged and predict the response for x = 6.

Hint

Change the final multiplication in main. The fit still sees the original four pairs.

Solution

The fitted coefficient is still 2, and multiplying by 6 produces 12.

Find

```blyx
slope * 5.0
```

Replace with

```blyx
slope * 6.0
```

Output after the change

```
2
12
```

### [Measure prediction error](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/model-error)

Evaluate a set of predictions, trace the residuals and interpret their mean squared error.

#### Compare paired observations

Take one prediction and the matching observed target. Their difference is a residual. Its sign tells you whether the prediction is high or low. Averaging signed residuals alone could hide errors that cancel one another.

#### Accumulate the loss

With predictions [2, 3, 5] and targets [1, 4, 3], the residuals are 1, -1 and 2. Squaring gives 1, 1 and 4. Add the squares, then divide 6 by the number of observations, 3. The mean squared error is 2.

#### Match types and lengths

The loop index is an integer for at. The floating-point count supplies a same-type divisor for squares in both execution paths. For inputs supplied by a caller, check that the lengths match and that at least one pair exists before you compute the mean.

#### Use held-out data

Training chooses a slope or other parameters. Evaluation asks how those fixed parameters perform on examples that did not determine them. Keep a second vector of test targets when comparing two models. A low training loss alone says little about unseen observations.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn main() {
    let predicted = [2.0, 3.0, 5.0];
    let target = [1.0, 4.0, 3.0];
    let mut squares = 0.0;
    let mut count = 0.0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(target) {
        let error = at(predicted, i) - at(target, i);
        squares += error * error;
        count += 1.0;
        i += 1;
    }
    println!(squares / count);
}
```

Expected output

```
2
```

#### Practice

Replace the predictions with the three actual targets. What is the best possible value of this loss?

Hint

Each residual should be exactly zero for these inputs.

Solution

All squared residuals are zero, so the mean squared error is zero.

Find

```blyx
[2.0, 3.0, 5.0]
```

Replace with

```blyx
[1.0, 4.0, 3.0]
```

Output after the change

```
0
```

### [Classify using a score and a threshold](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/classification)

Combine two features, choose a category, and decide how ties are classified.

#### Build the score

A feature is a numeric input such as a count or a measurement. A weight describes its contribution to a score. classify uses one weight per feature, computes dot(features, weights), then adds a scalar bias. The inputs and weights must have equal lengths.

#### Trace the prediction

The two contributions are 2 × 0.5 = 1 and 3 × -0.25 = -0.75. With a zero bias the score is 0.25. The condition score >= 0.0 chooses the string positive. A negative sign on a weight makes a larger feature lower the score.

#### Choose the tie rule

The comparison includes exactly zero on the positive side. A negative bias moves the cutoff without changing any individual weight. Test scores on both sides of zero and exactly at zero to check that the rule matches your intention.

#### Separate scoring from training

This is inference with coefficients supplied in the program. There is no learning step in this classifier. If you choose different coefficients, evaluate their predictions on labeled data before interpreting the change as an improvement.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn classify(features: vector, weights: vector, bias: f64) -> str {
    if dot(features, weights) + bias >= 0.0 {
        "positive"
    } else {
        "negative"
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!(classify([2.0, 3.0], [0.5, -0.25], 0.0));
}
```

Expected output

```
positive
```

#### Practice

Set the bias to -0.5 and predict the label before running.

Hint

The original weighted sum is 0.25.

Solution

The adjusted score is -0.25. This selects the negative branch.

Find

```blyx
[0.5, -0.25], 0.0
```

Replace with

```blyx
[0.5, -0.25], -0.5
```

Output after the change

```
negative
```

## Practical projects

### [Test a program at its boundaries](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/testing)

Design a small repeatable test suite that catches an off-by-one classification rule.

#### Write the rule first

Raise an alarm only above 30.0. This sentence decides what happens at exactly 30.0. Implement the production rule in a function so the test calls precisely the same calculation that a larger program would use.

#### Choose three cases

Select a value below the limit, exactly at the limit, and above it. For each input, compare the returned boolean with the expected boolean. A correct run prints true three times. If one line prints false, its position identifies the case to inspect.

#### Prove a test can fail

Temporarily replace > with >= and run again. The below and above cases still pass. The equality case now prints false. Restore the strict comparison and repeat. This gives you evidence that at least one test can detect a real defect.

#### Compare execution paths

Run the same source with blyxc run, then build an executable and compare its output on the same inputs. Checking the process exit status detects execution failures. Checking actual output against expected output detects wrong answers from executions that finished successfully.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn alarm(t: f64) -> bool {
    t > 30.0
}

fn main() {
    println!(alarm(29.5) == false);
    println!(alarm(30.0) == false);
    println!(alarm(30.5) == true);
}
```

Expected output

```
true
true
true
```

#### Practice

Change the rule to include exactly 30 and update the expected result for that input.

Hint

The implementation and the test expectation express two sides of the same contract.

Solution

Both changes are needed to keep all three tests passing under the new specification.

Find

```blyx
t > 30.0
```

Replace with

```blyx
t >= 30.0
```

Find

```blyx
alarm(30.0) == false
```

Replace with

```blyx
alarm(30.0) == true
```

Output after the change

```
true
true
true
```

### [Capstone project — build a sensor report](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/sensor-report)

Build a complete report from a blank file, handle empty input, and verify a boundary condition.

#### Specify the report

Given a vector of readings and a limit, print their total and how many exceed the limit. For an empty batch, print no readings and stop. Before coding, write down the expected behavior for an empty batch, one reading equal to the limit, and a batch with readings on both sides.

#### Build the counting function

Start with fn hot_count(readings: vector, limit: f64) -> i64. Start hits and i at zero. While i is less than len(readings), inspect at(readings, i). Increment hits only for a reading strictly above the limit. Advance i on every pass and return hits after the loop.

#### Build the report function

Take the same two parameters. Check for an empty batch first. The early return lets the normal report follow at the same indentation. Use sum for the total, call hot_count for the count, and pair print! labels with println! values.

#### Trace and verify

The four readings total 123.5. Only 31.5 and 34.0 exceed the limit of 30.0. The empty batch exercises a separate branch without reading an element. Verify the complete program in both the browser and the CLI.

| Input | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| [] | One line: no readings |
| [30.0] with limit 30.0 | Total 30 and count 0 |
| [28.0, 31.5, 30.0, 34.0] with limit 30.0 | Total 123.5 and count 2 |

#### Take it further

Change the function to count readings inside an inclusive range. Accept low and high parameters and combine two comparisons with &&. Test both endpoints, a value outside each end, and an empty vector. Decide how a caller should handle low greater than high.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn hot_count(readings: vector, limit: f64) -> i64 {
    let mut hits = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(readings) {
        if at(readings, i) > limit { hits += 1; }
        i += 1;
    }
    hits
}

fn report(readings: vector, limit: f64) {
    if len(readings) == 0 {
        println!("no readings");
        return;
    }
    print!("total: ");
    println!(sum(readings));
    print!("above limit: ");
    println!(hot_count(readings, limit));
}

fn main() {
    report([28.0, 31.5, 30.0, 34.0], 30.0);
    report([], 30.0);
}
```

Expected output

```
total: 123.5
above limit: 2
no readings
```

#### Practice

Replace only the empty batch in main with a single reading equal to the limit. Predict the complete report.

Hint

This batch takes the nonempty branch but adds nothing to the above-limit count.

Solution

The first batch is unchanged. For the second, sum returns 30 and the strict comparison leaves hits at zero.

Find

```blyx
report([], 30.0);
```

Replace with

```blyx
report([30.0], 30.0);
```

Output after the change

```
total: 123.5
above limit: 2
total: 30
above limit: 0
```

### [Evaluate models with Blyx packages](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/ai-packages)

Compare the cost of two classifiers, check their probability forecasts, and score a ranked retrieval result. Run the comparison in CI or import the same Blyx functions into your application.

#### Start with a release decision

You have predictions from two versions of a classifier on the same held-out observations. The current model raises one false alarm. Its replacement misses one positive. Both get three out of four right. Decide what a false alarm and a miss cost before you look at which model wins.

#### Prepare a paired CSV

Save the four rows below as predictions.csv in UTF-8. Each row must refer to the same observation for both models. The label is 0 or 1. Each prediction is an unquoted number between 0 and 1. Keep the header and column order shown. Rows can use LF or CRLF line endings.

```
label,baseline,candidate
1,0.9,0.4
1,0.8,0.9
0,0.6,0.2
0,0.1,0.1
```

#### Run ModelGate

ModelGate 0.1.2 ships as a native executable. On Apple Silicon macOS or x86-64 Linux use the Homebrew command below. On x64 Windows, extract the release ZIP from the ecosystem catalog and run .\modelgate.exe predictions.csv --fn-cost 5 in PowerShell. A release archive also contains fixtures/improved.csv and fixtures/regression.csv.

```
brew install rahulchaube1/blyx/modelgate
modelgate predictions.csv --fn-cost 5
```

#### Read the decision

At the default threshold of 0.5, a score equal to the threshold counts as positive. The baseline’s one false alarm costs 1. The candidate’s missed positive costs 5. Divide by four observations to get costs per row of 0.25 and 1.25. The JSON pass field is false. You can retain the report as a CI artifact using shell output redirection.

| Exit code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Candidate meets the cost and Brier criteria. |
| 1 | The candidate exceeds at least one permitted limit. |
| 2 | The CSV, a value or a command option is invalid. Check the diagnostic. |
| 4 | The native host could not complete an I/O operation. |

#### Measure probability quality

Brier score averages the squared difference between each probability and its binary label. Two models with identical class decisions can have different Brier scores. ModelGate accepts --brier-tolerance for the largest allowed increase in this mean. The calibration library also provides cal_bin for counts, forecast totals and outcome totals, and cal_ece for a count-weighted summary of the gaps. Compare ECE on the same data using the same bin count.

#### Import a versioned library

Install Blyx 0.2.1, Rust 1.85 or later and a platform linker for a source build. In an empty project directory, run the clone command below. It puts the release beside the entry file. For a shared project, record the commit in version control, for example as a Git submodule.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.1 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-classification.git vendor/classification
```

#### Use the library in a native program

Save this code as main.blyx beside vendor and run blyxc native-run main.blyx. It prints 6, the total cost of one false alarm and one miss. To keep the executable use blyxc build main.blyx -o evaluate, or -o evaluate.exe on Windows. The editable browser program below contains the same library in one file.

```
use vendor::classification::classification;

fn main() {
    println!(class_cost(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 5.0));
}
```

#### Evaluate a retriever

Use the retrieval package to score an ordered list of numeric document IDs for one judged query. With results [7, 7, 9], judgments [7, 9] and k of 3, unique hits occur at ranks 1 and 3. Precision is 2/3, recall is 1, reciprocal rank is 1, and average precision is (1 + 2/3) / 2. A repeated document still uses a rank. Record which queries have judgments and average the per-query metrics over that set.

#### Keep future data out of a time-series backtest

Blyx Backtest measures forecasts in chronological folds. For demand [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80], set initial history to 3, forecast horizon to 2, gap to 1 and training window to 2. The first fold trains on 20 and 30, skips 40 and scores against 50 and 60. The next trains on 40 and 50, skips 60 and scores against 70 and 80. Across those four observations the last-value baseline has mean absolute error of 25, the training-mean baseline 30, and custom forecasts [45, 55, 65, 75] score 5. Use the same fold bounds when fitting preprocessing and model parameters.

```
let scores = bt_baselines([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80], 3, 2, 1, 2);
```

#### Choose what to test

Use held-out paired data and keep the error costs, threshold and tolerance fixed when comparing runs. Inspect the individual errors and the number of observations. The four-row fixture illustrates the decision rule. Statistical uncertainty, subgroup performance and business impact require evidence from your own evaluation.

#### Worked program

```blyx
// Single-file example from https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-classification/tree/v0.1.1
// Rows in a confusion vector are [true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives].
pub fn class_probability(score: f64) -> bool {
    score >= 0.0 && score <= 1.0
}

pub fn class_label(value: f64) -> bool {
    value == 0.0 || value == 1.0
}

pub fn class_positive(score: f64, threshold: f64) -> bool {
    score >= threshold
}

pub fn class_confusion(labels: vector, scores: vector, threshold: f64) -> vector {
    if len(labels) == 0 || len(labels) != len(scores) || !class_probability(threshold) { return []; }
    let mut tp = 0.0;
    let mut fp = 0.0;
    let mut tn = 0.0;
    let mut missed = 0.0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(labels) {
        let label = at(labels, i);
        let score = at(scores, i);
        if !class_label(label) || !class_probability(score) { return []; }
        if class_positive(score, threshold) {
            if label == 1.0 { tp += 1.0; } else { fp += 1.0; }
        } else {
            if label == 1.0 { missed += 1.0; } else { tn += 1.0; }
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    [tp, fp, tn, missed]
}

fn ratio(numerator: f64, denominator: f64) -> f64 {
    if denominator == 0.0 { return 0.0; }
    numerator / denominator
}

pub fn class_precision(tp: f64, fp: f64) -> f64 { ratio(tp, tp + fp) }
pub fn class_recall(tp: f64, missed: f64) -> f64 { ratio(tp, tp + missed) }
pub fn class_f1(tp: f64, fp: f64, missed: f64) -> f64 { ratio(2.0 * tp, 2.0 * tp + fp + missed) }
pub fn class_cost(fp: f64, missed: f64, fp_cost: f64, fn_cost: f64) -> f64 {
    fp * fp_cost + missed * fn_cost
}

fn main() {
    let table = class_confusion([1, 0, 1, 0], [0.9, 0.6, 0.4, 0.1], 0.5);
    println!(class_precision(at(table, 0), at(table, 1)));
    println!(class_recall(at(table, 0), at(table, 3)));
    println!(class_cost(at(table, 1), at(table, 3), 1.0, 5.0));
}
```

Expected output

```
0.5
0.5
6
```

#### Practice

In the worked program, raise the cost of a missed positive from 5 to 10. Predict the three lines of output and then run it.

Hint

Only the total cost uses that argument. The confusion counts stay the same.

Solution

Precision and recall both remain 0.5. One false alarm costs 1 and one missed positive now costs 10, so the final line is 11.

Find

```blyx
at(table, 3), 1.0, 5.0
```

Replace with

```blyx
at(table, 3), 1.0, 10.0
```

Output after the change

```
0.5
0.5
11
```

### [Train, calibrate and monitor a regression model](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/training-and-monitoring)

Fit a regression, attach intervals using held-out errors, and catch persistent underprediction in a later stream. Run each stage in native Blyx or the browser.

#### Keep three sets of observations

Use training pairs to fit the model. Reserve a separate calibration set for choosing an interval radius. Keep a stable, chronological reference period and later labelled predictions for monitoring. Reusing training errors for calibration can make intervals too narrow. Choose data splits before fitting.

#### Fit the relationship

Save x,y pairs as a UTF-8 CSV. The second column is the response. The four rows below follow y = 2x + 1. The centered least-squares fit has feature mean 2.5, response mean 6 and slope 2. At x = 5 it predicts 11.

```
x,y
1,3
2,5
3,7
4,9
```

#### Run LinearFit

Extract the LinearFit archive for your platform and run the included fixture. On Windows, start the command with .\linearfit.exe in PowerShell. On Apple Silicon macOS and x86-64 Linux you can also install it from the Blyx Homebrew tap. Supplying --ridge 5 shrinks the slope to 1 and changes the prediction to 8.5.

```
./linearfit fixtures/line.csv --predict 5
```

#### Train by batch or by row

Use lf_fit on aligned vectors for a batch. For incoming observations start with lf_start, pass the state and next training pair to lf_update, and call lf_finish when you need a model. lf_merge combines disjoint training batches. The shared Moments library also exposes their means, centered sums and sample standard deviation.

#### Calibrate an interval

Suppose a separate model predicted 10 for each of four calibration cases whose true values were 10, 12, 7 and 11. The absolute errors are 0, 2, 3 and 1. At target coverage 3/5, take the third smallest error because ceil((4+1)×3/5) = 3. This yields a radius of 2 and the interval [18,22] around a new prediction of 20. At 90% coverage four cases give no finite result.

```
let cal = cf_calibrate([10, 12, 7, 11], [10, 10, 10, 10], 3, 5);
let interval = cf_interval(20.0, at(cal, 0));
```

#### Interpret coverage

Use cf_coverage on separate labelled predictions to measure the fraction inside the intervals. The usual split-conformal guarantee is marginal and assumes calibration and future examples are exchangeable. Inspect time periods or important subgroups separately when that assumption may fail.

#### Detect sustained underprediction

ResidualWatch calculates actual minus predicted. In its shift fixture the first three residuals are −1, 0 and 1, so the frozen center is 0 and the sample scale is 1. Two later residuals of 2 add 1.5 each to the positive CUSUM at allowance 0.5. The second reaches the inclusive limit of 3. The first alert is data row 5, and the CLI exits with status 1.

```
./residualwatch fixtures/shift.csv --reference 3 --limit 3
```

#### Use alerts in a job

Keep the JSON report from each run. Exit code 0 means the monitor finished without an alert, 1 means a limit was reached, 2 signals invalid input and 4 signals an I/O failure. Choose an allowance, limit and scale floor using a representative stable period. Investigate drift alarms against labels and feature changes before deciding whether to retrain.

#### Add a package to a native project

With Blyx 0.2.1, Rust and a host linker installed, clone the tagged release next to your entry file. The training and monitoring packages include their pinned Blyx dependencies. Save the imported program as main.blyx and run blyxc native-run main.blyx. The package catalog has the exact import, function reference, runnable example and source for every package.

```
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.1.1 https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-linearfit.git vendor/linearfit

# First line of main.blyx
use vendor::linearfit::linearfit;
```

#### Run all three stages in one project

The starter includes LinearFit, Conformal, ResidualWatch and their Blyx dependencies. With the native toolchain installed, extract the ZIP and run the command below in the project folder. The model predicts 21 with an interval from 19 to 23. The first incoming error gives a signal of 0. A second underprediction raises the signal to 1.

```
blyxc native-run main.blyx
```

[Download the starter project](https://www.blyx-lang.space/examples/forecast-monitor.zip) · [Read the source on GitHub](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxxxx/tree/blyx-main/examples/ml/forecast-monitor)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-moments/blob/v0.1.0/moments.blyx
// A paired summary stores [count, mean_x, mean_y, Sxx, Sxy, Syy].
fn moments_finite(x: f64) -> bool { x - x == 0.0 }

pub fn mom_empty() -> vector { [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] }

pub fn mom_valid(s: vector) -> bool {
    if len(s) != 6 { return false; }
    let n = at(s, 0);
    if !(n >= 0.0 && n <= 9007199254740991.0) || n % 1.0 != 0.0 { return false; }
    let mut i = 1;
    while i < 6 {
        if !moments_finite(at(s, i)) || (n == 0.0 && at(s, i) != 0.0) { return false; }
        i += 1;
    }
    at(s, 3) >= 0.0 && at(s, 5) >= 0.0
}

pub fn mom_update(s: vector, x: f64, y: f64) -> vector {
    if !mom_valid(s) || !moments_finite(x) || !moments_finite(y) { return []; }
    if at(s, 0) == 0.0 { return [1, x, y, 0, 0, 0]; }
    let n = at(s, 0) + 1.0;
    let dx = x - at(s, 1);
    let dy = y - at(s, 2);
    let mx = at(s, 1) + dx / n;
    let my = at(s, 2) + dy / n;
    let next = [n, mx, my, at(s, 3) + dx * (x - mx),
                at(s, 4) + dx * (y - my), at(s, 5) + dy * (y - my)];
    if !mom_valid(next) { return []; }
    next
}

pub fn mom_summary(x: vector, y: vector) -> vector {
    if len(x) != len(y) { return []; }
    let mut state = mom_empty();
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < len(x) {
        state = mom_update(state, at(x, i), at(y, i));
        if len(state) == 0 { return []; }
        i += 1;
    }
    state
}

pub fn mom_merge(a: vector, b: vector) -> vector {
    if !mom_valid(a) || !mom_valid(b) { return []; }
    if at(a, 0) == 0.0 { return b; }
    if at(b, 0) == 0.0 { return a; }
    let n = at(a, 0) + at(b, 0);
    let share = at(b, 0) / n;
    let weight = at(a, 0) * share;
    let dx = at(b, 1) - at(a, 1);
    let dy = at(b, 2) - at(a, 2);
    let next = [n, at(a, 1) + dx * share, at(a, 2) + dy * share,
                (at(a, 3) + at(b, 3)) + (dx * weight) * dx,
                (at(a, 4) + at(b, 4)) + (dx * weight) * dy,
                (at(a, 5) + at(b, 5)) + (dy * weight) * dy];
    if !mom_valid(next) { return []; }
    next
}

// Reduce to [1,4) before Newton iteration, including for subnormal variance.
fn moments_positive_root(value: f64) -> f64 {
    if value == 0.0 { return 0.0; }
    let mut v = value;
    let mut factor = 1.0;
    while v >= 4.0 { v /= 4.0; factor *= 2.0; }
    while v < 1.0 { v *= 4.0; factor /= 2.0; }
    let mut root = 2.0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < 6 { root = 0.5 * (root + v / root); i += 1; }
    root * factor
}

pub fn mom_sample_sd_y(s: vector) -> f64 {
    if !mom_valid(s) || at(s, 0) < 2.0 { return -1.0; }
    moments_positive_root(at(s, 5) / (at(s, 0) - 1.0))
}

// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyx-linearfit/blob/v0.1.1/linearfit.blyx
fn linearfit_finite(x: f64) -> bool { x - x == 0.0 }

pub fn lf_start() -> vector { mom_empty() }
pub fn lf_update(s: vector, x: f64, y: f64) -> vector { mom_update(s, x, y) }
pub fn lf_merge(a: vector, b: vector) -> vector { mom_merge(a, b) }

// Model is centered at the sample means to preserve precision in prediction.
// penalty multiplies slope squared in the unnormalized sum-of-squares objective.
pub fn lf_finish(s: vector, penalty: f64) -> vector {
    if !mom_valid(s) || at(s, 0) < 2.0 || !linearfit_finite(penalty) || penalty < 0.0 { return []; }
    let denominator = at(s, 3) + penalty;
    if denominator <= 0.0 || !linearfit_finite(denominator) { return []; }
    let slope = at(s, 4) / denominator;
    if !linearfit_finite(slope) { return []; }
    [at(s, 1), at(s, 2), slope]
}

pub fn lf_fit(x: vector, y: vector, penalty: f64) -> vector {
    lf_finish(mom_summary(x, y), penalty)
}

pub fn lf_predict(model: vector, x: f64) -> f64 {
    if len(model) != 3 || !linearfit_finite(x) { return 0.0 / 0.0; }
    let y = at(model, 1) + at(model, 2) * (x - at(model, 0));
    if !linearfit_finite(y) { return 0.0 / 0.0; }
    y
}

fn main() {
    let training = lf_fit([1, 2, 3, 4], [3, 5, 7, 9], 0.0);
    println!(at(training, 2));
    println!(lf_predict(training, 5.0));
}
```

Expected output

```
2
11
```

#### Practice

In the worked program, change the training penalty from 0 to 5. What happens to the slope and the prediction at x = 5?

Hint

Sxx is 5 and Sxy is 10. The ridge slope divides Sxy by Sxx plus the penalty.

Solution

The slope becomes 1. The centered prediction is 6 + 1 × (5 − 2.5), or 8.5.

Find

```blyx
[3, 5, 7, 9], 0.0);
```

Replace with

```blyx
[3, 5, 7, 9], 5.0);
```

Output after the change

```
1
8.5
```

### [Train a neural network with BlyxTorch](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/blyxtorch)

Train an XOR classifier, inspect a real gradient, then compile a dense network for your own labels and deploy it as a standalone CPU executable.

#### Learn a nonlinear decision

XOR labels the input pair (0,1) or (1,0) as positive. A single straight-line decision boundary cannot separate both positive points from the two negative points. The default BlyxTorch model uses two inputs, four tanh hidden units and one output logit. Its 17 parameters include all weights and biases.

#### Train the released classifier

Download and extract the matching archive. From its folder, run the three commands below. Training takes 250 epochs with Adam, a learning rate of 0.03, batches of four and seed 7. The output is a two-line text checkpoint. The prebuilt trainer runs directly. On Windows PowerShell, start commands with .\blyxtorch.exe and save the checkpoint with | Out-File -Encoding ascii xor.bt.

```
./blyxtorch train fixtures/xor.csv 250 0.03 4 adam 7 > xor.bt
./blyxtorch predict xor.bt fixtures/xor-features.csv
./blyxtorch score xor.bt fixtures/xor.csv
```

[Download the native release](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxtorch/releases/tag/v0.1.0) · [Read the framework source](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxtorch)

#### Read the predictions

The mean training loss is about 0.00630 on the four rows. The probabilities below are rounded. To evaluate performance on a real dataset, keep separate labelled observations out of training and run score on those rows. In the browser example, change the second input from [0, 1] to [0, 0]. Its predicted class changes from true to false.

[Run the trained XOR network in your browser](https://www.blyx-lang.space/play?example=package-blyxtorch-xor)

| x0 | x1 | Target | Probability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0.00365 |
| 0 | 1 | 1 | 0.99391 |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0.99308 |
| 1 | 1 | 0 | 0.00846 |

#### Trace a derivative

The browser program uses a dual number with a value and a tangent. For a trainable weight use tangent 1; for a constant use tangent 0. At w = 1, the loss (2w − 5)² is 9. Its derivative is −12, so a gradient step with learning rate 0.125 moves the weight to 2.5 and the loss becomes zero.

#### Compile a different network

Widths include input and output. This example uses eight and four hidden units for a three-class classifier. Compile the emitted Blyx source with Blyx 0.2.1, Rust 1.85 or later and a host linker. The resulting executable can train and predict on a different machine of the same target platform. For Windows PowerShell, send the emitted source through Out-File -Encoding ascii classifier.blyx and compile to classifier.exe.

```
./blyxtorch emit 2,8,4,3 softmax relu > classifier.blyx
blyxc build classifier.blyx -o classifier
./classifier --help
```

#### Choose a loss and a header

Use mse for continuous targets, binary for one probability, or softmax for a single class index per observation. The input is an unquoted numerical UTF-8 CSV. Training and gradient commands use labelled rows. Prediction takes the feature columns alone.

| Task | Example header | Model output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two regression targets | x0,x1,y0,y1 | Two real numbers |
| Binary classification | x0,x1,y0 | One probability |
| Three-class classification | x0,x1,class | Three probabilities summing to one |

#### Inspect gradients and checkpoints

The gradient command returns a per-row loss followed by one derivative per trainable weight or bias. The compiled backward pass uses the chain rule to traverse the layers in reverse order. Within each layer the output-by-input weight matrix comes first in row-major order, then its bias vector. Loading checks the model's identity and parameter count. The optimizer uses the actual size of the final mini-batch.

```
./blyxtorch gradient xor.bt fixtures/xor.csv
```

#### Choose an appropriate workload

BlyxTorch 0.1.0 runs fixed-shape float64 networks on CPU. It supports up to eight affine layers and 1,024 parameters. The published comparison covers five small networks, CPU PyTorch, and a separate CSV-scoring benchmark. GPU execution, convolution, transformer training and arbitrary-rank tensors are outside this release.

[Compare the timings and measurement boundaries](https://www.blyx-lang.space/benchmarks#blyxtorch) · [Inspect the PyTorch numerical comparisons](https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxtorch/blob/v0.1.0/verification/parity.json)

#### Worked program

```blyx
// BlyxTorch 0.1.0, MIT OR Apache-2.0.
// https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/blyxtorch
fn main() {
    let weight = bt_dual(1.0, 1.0);
    let x = bt_dual(2.0, 0.0);
    let target = bt_dual(5.0, 0.0);
    let loss = bt_square(bt_sub(bt_mul(weight, x), target));
    println!(at(loss, 0));
    println!(at(loss, 1));
    let updated = bt_dual(at(weight, 0) - 0.125 * at(loss, 1), 0.0);
    println!(at(bt_square(bt_sub(bt_mul(updated, x), target)), 0));
}

// Portable f64 primitives and forward-mode automatic differentiation.
pub fn btx_finite(x: f64) -> bool { x - x == 0.0 }
pub fn btx_valid(v: vector, width: i64) -> bool {
    if len(v) != width { return false; }
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < width {
        if !btx_finite(at(v, i)) { return false; }
        i += 1;
    }
    true
}

// exp(-x) for finite x >= 0. Range reduction bounds the Taylor remainder.
fn exp_decay(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x >= 746.0 { return 0.0; }
    let mut r = -x;
    let mut levels = 0;
    while r < -0.35 { r *= 0.5; levels += 1; }
    let mut term = 1.0;
    let mut total = 1.0;
    let mut k = 1.0;
    while k <= 15.0 { term *= r / k; total += term; k += 1.0; }
    while levels > 0 { total *= total; levels -= 1; }
    total
}
pub fn btx_exp_shift(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x > 0.0 { return 0.0 / 0.0; }
    exp_decay(-x)
}

// log(1+x), 0 <= x <= 1. The transformed series also retains very small x.
fn log1p_unit(x: f64) -> f64 {
    let z = x / (2.0 + x);
    let zz = z * z;
    let mut term = z;
    let mut accum = z;
    let mut k = 3.0;
    while k <= 35.0 { term *= zz; accum += term / k; k += 2.0; }
    2.0 * accum
}
// The softmax denominator is always finite and at least one.
pub fn btx_log_sum(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x < 1.0 || !btx_finite(x) { return 0.0 / 0.0; }
    let mut n = x;
    let mut offset = 0.0;
    while n >= 2.0 { n *= 0.5; offset += 0.6931471805599453; }
    offset + log1p_unit(n - 1.0)
}
pub fn btx_sqrt(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x == 0.0 { return 0.0; }
    if x < 0.0 || !btx_finite(x) { return 0.0 / 0.0; }
    let mut z = x;
    let mut scale = 1.0;
    while z < 1.0 { z *= 4.0; scale *= 0.5; }
    while z > 4.0 { z *= 0.25; scale *= 2.0; }
    let mut r = 1.5;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < 6 { r = 0.5 * (r + z / r); i += 1; }
    r * scale
}
pub fn btx_logistic(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x >= 0.0 { return 1.0 / (1.0 + exp_decay(x)); }
    let q = exp_decay(-x);
    q / (1.0 + q)
}
pub fn btx_tanh_value(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x < 0.0 { return -btx_tanh_value(-x); }
    if x < 0.00001 { return x * (1.0 - x*x/3.0); }
    let q = exp_decay(2.0*x);
    (1.0-q)/(1.0+q)
}
pub fn btx_relu_value(x: f64) -> f64 { if x > 0.0 { return x; } 0.0 }
pub fn btx_softplus_value(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x >= 0.0 { return x + log1p_unit(exp_decay(x)); }
    log1p_unit(exp_decay(-x))
}
pub fn btx_bce_value(logit: f64, label: f64) -> f64 {
    if logit >= 0.0 { return (1.0-label)*logit + log1p_unit(exp_decay(logit)); }
    return -label*logit + log1p_unit(exp_decay(-logit));
}
pub fn btx_bce_slope(logit: f64, label: f64) -> f64 {
    if logit >= 0.0 { return (1.0-label) - btx_logistic(-logit); }
    btx_logistic(logit) - label
}
pub fn bt_dual(value: f64, tangent: f64) -> vector {
    if !btx_finite(value) || !btx_finite(tangent) { return []; }
    [value, tangent]
}
pub fn bt_add(a: vector, b: vector) -> vector {
    if len(a) != 2 || len(b) != 2 { return []; }
    bt_dual(at(a,0)+at(b,0), at(a,1)+at(b,1))
}
pub fn bt_sub(a: vector, b: vector) -> vector {
    if len(a) != 2 || len(b) != 2 { return []; }
    bt_dual(at(a,0)-at(b,0), at(a,1)-at(b,1))
}
pub fn bt_mul(a: vector, b: vector) -> vector {
    if len(a) != 2 || len(b) != 2 { return []; }
    bt_dual(at(a,0)*at(b,0), at(a,1)*at(b,0) + at(a,0)*at(b,1))
}
pub fn bt_div(a: vector, b: vector) -> vector {
    if len(a) != 2 || len(b) != 2 || at(b,0) == 0.0 { return []; }
    let v = at(a,0)/at(b,0);
    bt_dual(v, (at(a,1)-v*at(b,1))/at(b,0))
}
pub fn bt_square(a: vector) -> vector { bt_mul(a, a) }
pub fn bt_relu(a: vector) -> vector {
    if !btx_valid(a,2) { return []; }
    if at(a,0) > 0.0 { return a; }
    [0,0]
}
pub fn bt_tanh(a: vector) -> vector {
    if !btx_valid(a,2) { return []; }
    let v = btx_tanh_value(at(a,0));
    bt_dual(v, (1.0-v)*(1.0+v)*at(a,1))
}
pub fn bt_sigmoid(a: vector) -> vector {
    if !btx_valid(a,2) { return []; }
    let x = at(a,0);
    bt_dual(btx_logistic(x), btx_logistic(x)*btx_logistic(-x)*at(a,1))
}
pub fn bt_softplus(a: vector) -> vector {
    if !btx_valid(a,2) { return []; }
    bt_dual(btx_softplus_value(at(a,0)), btx_logistic(at(a,0))*at(a,1))
}
pub fn bt_bce_logits(a: vector, label: f64) -> vector {
    if !btx_valid(a,2) || !btx_finite(label) || label < 0.0 || label > 1.0 { return []; }
    bt_dual(btx_bce_value(at(a,0),label), btx_bce_slope(at(a,0),label)*at(a,1))
}
```

Expected output

```
9
-12
0
```

#### Practice

In the worked program, change the learning rate from 0.125 to 0.25. Where does the update put the weight, and what loss do you get?

Hint

The derivative before the update is −12. Compute 1 − 0.25 × (−12), then square the new prediction error.

Solution

The weight becomes 4. Its prediction is 8, so the new loss is (8 − 5)² = 9. The larger step crosses the minimum.

Find

```blyx
0.125 * at(loss, 1)
```

Replace with

```blyx
0.25 * at(loss, 1)
```

Output after the change

```
9
-12
9
```

## Local toolchain

### [Install and verify Blyx](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/installation)

Choose a binary or package manager, locate the executable, and verify the exact compiler version.

#### Choose how to run the course

Every tutorial with an editor can run in the browser. A local installation lets you save source files and invoke the command-line tool blyxc. Building a native executable also requires rustc and a host linker on the machine doing the build.

#### Download a release archive

Choose the Windows x86-64 ZIP, Linux x86-64 tarball, or Apple Silicon macOS tarball from the download page. Compare its SHA-256 digest with the entry for the same filename in SHA256SUMS. Extract the archive and add the directory containing blyxc to PATH. In PowerShell you can run .\blyxc.exe directly from the extracted directory.

#### Install with Homebrew

On Apple Silicon macOS or x86-64 Linux, the project tap installs the published compiler binary and checks the archive checksum.

```
brew install rahulchaube1/blyx/blyx
```

#### Install on Windows with Scoop

On Windows x64, add the project bucket once from PowerShell, then install the compiler and check its version. Scoop checks the release archive against the SHA-256 in the manifest. You can also install the native AI commands with scoop install blyx/linearfit blyx/residualwatch blyx/modelgate.

```
scoop bucket add blyx https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/scoop-blyx
scoop install blyx/blyx
blyxc --version
```

#### Install with Cargo

With Rust, Cargo and a host linker installed, build the compiler from crates.io. The version flag selects the same release as this course. Cargo normally places the result in the bin directory under your Cargo home.

```
cargo install --locked --version 0.2.1 blyxc
```

#### Check your installation

Open a fresh terminal after a PATH change. The version command should print blyxc 0.2.1. If the shell cannot find it, check the directory from which the executable runs directly and make sure that directory appears on PATH.

```
blyxc --version
```

#### Practice

Confirm which compiler your terminal will use if you have both a downloaded binary and a Cargo installation.

Hint

Use Get-Command blyxc in PowerShell or command -v blyxc in a POSIX shell.

Solution

The path should point to the installation you intended. Run that path with --version to verify it before continuing.

### [Create a project on disk](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/projects)

Move a program from the browser into a project, check the file and run it from a terminal.

#### Create a workspace

Choose a parent directory where you want to keep your work. This command creates a fresh directory named hello. Blyx refuses to create the project if that directory already exists, which helps protect existing work.

```
blyxc new hello
```

#### Find the entry point

The generated project contains Blyx.toml and src/main.blyx. The manifest records the project name, version and edition. The released CLI takes an explicit source file. Open hello/src/main.blyx in a text editor and find fn main().

#### Check, run and edit

From the same parent directory, run these commands in order. check parses the source. run executes it. The starter prints Hello, Blyx! Replace its print call with a calculation, save the file and run it again.

```
blyxc check hello/src/main.blyx
blyxc run hello/src/main.blyx
```

#### Keep paths consistent

If you change directory into hello, write src/main.blyx in subsequent commands. A file-not-found message is often a working-directory issue. The formatter rewrites the named file with normalized line endings.

```
blyxc fmt hello/src/main.blyx
```

#### Add a package to a native project

Clone a tagged Blyx library beside your entry file and import its public functions with use. The native runner and native build follow these local paths. The “Evaluate models with Blyx packages” chapter builds a working example. A Git submodule or a recorded commit keeps the dependency reproducible.

#### Practice

Make the starter print 21. Run a syntax check first and then execute the saved file.

Hint

In main, multiply 3 by 7 inside println!.

Solution

Use println!(3 * 7); and save. A successful check reports that the file parsed. The run command prints 21.

### [Develop in VS Code](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/editor)

Run an unsaved editor buffer, read a parser diagnostic and move the same program to the CLI.

#### Open a Blyx file

Install the desktop extension with ID RahulChaube.blyx-language. Open or create a file ending in .blyx. For an untitled buffer, select Blyx as its language. The editor highlighting helps you see strings, keywords and comments.

#### Run the active buffer

Use the play button in the editor title bar or choose Blyx: Run File in the Command Palette. The Blyx output channel shows the output for the current text, including unsaved edits. Paste the first tutorial program and change the string to confirm which version is running.

#### Read a diagnostic

Remove the closing brace of main and look in the Problems panel. A parser diagnostic reports where parsing ran into trouble. Restore the brace, wait for the parser to update and run again. Runtime failures, such as a zero integer divisor, appear when the program executes.

#### Use a local extension file

For an offline installation, download blyx-language-1.2.3.vsix from the editor release and choose Install from VSIX in the Extensions view. The extension uses a bundled WebAssembly interpreter. Save the source to disk before running a CLI command against that file.

#### Practice

Change a string without saving. Compare an editor run with a terminal run before and after saving.

Hint

The editor reads the buffer. The terminal reads the file on disk.

Solution

Before saving, the editor can print the new string while the CLI prints the old one. Save and run both again to compare the same source.

### [Debug and recover from errors](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/diagnostics)

Locate a syntax error, diagnose a runtime failure, and guard an operation using short-circuit evaluation.

#### Identify the failing stage

Check the file path first. A syntax error occurs while reading the program structure. A runtime error occurs while executing a valid expression with particular values. An error from a native build can point to a type mismatch or a missing Rust toolchain.

| Observation | Likely cause | First action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A parser line and column | Missing punctuation or an unfinished expression | Inspect that token and the preceding statement. |
| index … out of bounds | The index fell outside the vector | Check 0 <= i and i < len(v) before at. |
| dot requires vectors of equal length | The inputs contain different numbers of observations | Compare both lengths. |
| step limit exceeded | The budget ran out | Trace the loop condition and its updates. |

#### Reproduce the smallest failure

Save fn main() { println!(1 / 0); } as divide.blyx. A syntax check succeeds because the expression is well formed. Running it reports an integer division error and exits with code 4. Replace the zero with 2 and rerun. Whole-number division now prints 0.

#### Put a guard before division

The example reads count != 0 && total / count > 3. With a zero count the first comparison is false, so evaluation skips the division. Reversing the operands would evaluate the division before discovering the zero.

#### Limit a test run

A runaway loop can repeatedly evaluate valid code. Use a small positive budget while investigating it. The released interpreter also enforces a separate call-depth limit. Increasing the budget only helps after you have confirmed that the computation progresses.

```
blyxc run src/main.blyx --max-steps 10000
```

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn above_limit(total: i64, count: i64) -> bool {
    count != 0 && total / count > 3
}

fn main() {
    println!(above_limit(12, 0));
    println!(above_limit(12, 2));
}
```

Expected output

```
false
true
```

#### Practice

Make the second call use a nonzero count whose integer quotient is exactly three.

Hint

Keep total at 12 and choose a count that divides it evenly.

Solution

The quotient 12 / 4 is 3. The strict > 3 comparison returns false, and the zero-count case also returns false.

Find

```blyx
above_limit(12, 2)
```

Replace with

```blyx
above_limit(12, 4)
```

Output after the change

```
false
false
```

### [Build a native executable](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/native-builds)

Compile a typed Blyx program and compare the executable with the interpreter on the same input.

#### Start with a known result

Run the project source through the interpreter and keep a small expected output. When trying a native build for the first time, use the generated hello project or the capstone. Both have simple results that you can check by eye.

#### Build for your host

Install a Rust compiler and host linker. From inside your Blyx project, run the command below. The native backend translates supported Blyx syntax to Rust and invokes rustc to produce an optimized executable for the build machine.

```
blyxc build src/main.blyx
```

#### Choose the output location

An explicit output name makes scripts easier to read. On Linux or macOS, run the executable using a relative path. Use a separate output path from the source file.

```
blyxc build src/main.blyx -o hello
./hello
```

#### Build on Windows

In PowerShell, use an .exe suffix and the current-directory prefix. The resulting executable runs independently of blyxc and rustc on a compatible machine.

```
blyxc build src/main.blyx -o hello.exe
.\hello.exe
```

#### Compare the two paths

Give numeric operands matching types and add explicit return types to functions that return values. The interpreter can promote mixed integer/float operations that a native build rejects. Check the executable's output using the same ordinary and boundary inputs you used for the interpreted run.

#### Build a program with imports

Native builds resolve local use paths and built-in host modules. The native runner builds the program and runs it in one step. Put program arguments after --. Use a normal build to keep an executable for repeated runs.

```
blyxc native-run src/main.blyx
```

#### Practice

Build the capstone source as a native executable, run it and compare the complete output with the chapter’s expected output.

Hint

Save the complete capstone program to src/main.blyx first.

Solution

The four readings sum to 123.5, two exceed 30, and the empty call prints no readings. Those three lines should agree across both execution paths.

## Language reference

### [Syntax, types and operators](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/language-reference)

Look up the executable forms, operator order and value types used in Blyx 0.2.1.

#### Read the shape of a program

A runnable source file declares top-level functions, including a parameterless main. A function body is a brace-delimited block of statements and an optional final expression. A semicolon ends a let declaration, return statement or expression statement. A final expression without one supplies the block’s value.

#### Read names, literals and comments

Choose a name such as sensor_count. Start with a letter or underscore and use letters, digits or underscores after it. Names are case-sensitive. The lexer reads 10, 0b1010, 0o12 and 0xA as the same integer. Use underscores to group long numbers and e for a decimal exponent. A line comment begins with //. A block comment begins with /* and ends with */. Block comments may nest.

#### Value types

Use explicit scalar types for native function parameters and results. Vector elements are numeric. A unit-valued block completes without returning a useful value.

| Type | Example | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| i64 | -12, 0, 42 | Checked integer arithmetic, counts and indices |
| f64 | 2.5, 1e-2 | Measurements, division with fractions and vector elements |
| bool | true, false | Conditions and logical combinations |
| str | "Blyx" | Text, labels and messages. The native subset also recognizes String. |
| vector | [2.0, 3.0] | An immutable sequence of numeric elements |
| unit (or omit the return annotation) | fn show() { println!(1); } | A function called for its effect |

#### Operator order

The rows are ordered from tightest binding to loosest among the operators used by the released interpreter here. Parentheses override the default order. Keep comparisons separate and join their boolean results with && or ||.

| Operators | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ! and unary - | Boolean negation and numeric negation | !ready, -x |
| * / % | Multiply, divide, remainder | 7 / 2 yields 3 |
| + - | Add, subtract | 2 + 3 * 4 yields 14 |
| < <= > >= | Order comparisons | t >= 30.0 |
| == != | Equality and inequality | count != 0 |
| && | Short-circuit logical AND | ready && valid |
| \|\| | Short-circuit logical OR | low \|\| high |
| = += -= *= /= %= | Assign to a mutable binding | count += 1 |

#### Declarations and control flow

let binds, let mut permits updates and fn introduces a function. if selects a branch, while checks before each pass, and loop repeats unconditionally. break leaves the nearest loop, continue begins its next iteration, and return exits the current function. Nested braces introduce a scope.

#### Literal and boundary behavior

The signed integer range is −9,223,372,036,854,775,808 through 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. Integer overflow and division by zero fail in the interpreter. f64 has finite precision and follows IEEE floating-point arithmetic. Many decimal fractions have only approximate binary representations. For native examples, use decimal literals consistently when a fractional result matters.

#### Text and escape sequences

Write strings in double quotes. Inside a string, \n starts a new line, \t inserts a tab, \" inserts a quote, and \\ inserts a backslash. Strings may contain Unicode text. Use several print! calls to combine text with values. The interpreter also reads a single-quoted character as one character of text. Use double-quoted text in code you plan to build natively.

#### Use a branch as a value

The classify function below uses if and else to produce a result. Both branch blocks end in string expressions and have the same result type. show returns unit and exists to print the result. The explicit -> unit annotation may be omitted there. Function parameters and any native return values use the types in the table above.

#### Worked program

```blyx
fn classify(n: i64) -> str {
    if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }
}

fn show() -> unit {
    /* The three literals represent the same count. */
    println!(0b1010 == 0xA && 0o12 == 10);
    println!(1_000 + 5);
    println!(2.5e1);
    print!("label\t");
    println!(classify(10));
}

fn main() {
    show();
}
```

Expected output

```
true
1005
25
label	even
```

#### Practice

Change the classifier call to use the integer eleven in hexadecimal. Predict the final line and check whether the other lines change.

Hint

In hexadecimal, the digits after 9 are A, B, C, D, E and F. Eleven divided by two leaves a remainder of one.

Solution

0xB is eleven. classify chooses the odd branch, and the earlier calculations still use the original literals.

Find

```blyx
classify(10)
```

Replace with

```blyx
classify(0xB)
```

Output after the change

```
true
1005
25
label	odd
```

### [Built-in functions and output](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/builtin-reference)

Look up every vector built-in and both output macros, including their inputs, results and boundary cases.

#### Vector operations

All four functions receive vectors by value in Blyx source. The interpreter shares immutable element storage across calls. An index is an i64; an element, sum or dot product is an f64.

| Call | Result | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| len(vector) | i64 count, zero for an empty vector | len([4.0, 9.0]) → 2 |
| at(vector, i64) | The element at a zero-based index | at([4.0, 9.0], 1) → 9 |
| sum(vector) | Sum of the elements | sum([4.0, 9.0]) → 13 |
| dot(vector, vector) | Sum of products at matching indices | dot([1.0, 2.0], [4.0, 9.0]) → 22 |

#### Preconditions

at fails on a negative index, on index len(v), and on any access to an empty vector. dot fails if lengths differ, even when one side is empty. The sum of an empty vector and the dot product of two empty vectors are numerically zero. Check lengths before indexing or computing an average.

#### Output macros

print!() emits no text. println!() emits a newline. With a single expression, print!(value) displays its value, and println!(value) follows it with a newline. Use consecutive calls to combine text and numbers. Braces inside an output string are literal characters.

#### Cost of the operations

Reading the length or one element requires no scan. sum and dot visit the elements and their work grows with vector length. The interpreter charges its execution budget for these reductions. Holding the sum in a binding avoids recomputing it in every loop iteration.

#### Practice

Calculate dot([2.0, -1.0], [3.0, 4.0]) by hand. What happens if you remove the 4.0 from the second vector?

Hint

Multiply the corresponding entries before summing.

Solution

2 × 3 + (−1 × 4) is 2. After removing an entry the lengths differ, and the runtime reports an error.

### [Command-line reference](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/cli-reference)

Look up CLI forms, output files, execution budgets and exit codes.

#### Command forms

Pass the entry file to each command. Native builds and native-run also load its local imports. Quote any path containing spaces as required by your shell.

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| blyxc --version or -V | Print the installed compiler version. |
| blyxc help, --help or -h | Show the available commands. |
| blyxc new NAME | Create a new directory with Blyx.toml and src/main.blyx. |
| blyxc check FILE | Parse the file and report syntax diagnostics. |
| blyxc run FILE [--max-steps N] | Interpret main with an optional positive step budget. |
| blyxc build FILE [-o PATH] | Build a native executable, optionally at PATH. |
| blyxc native-run FILE [-- ARGS...] | Build the native project, run it and forward the program arguments. |
| blyxc fmt FILE | Rewrite the file with normalized line endings. |

#### Interpret the exit status

Capture the exit status immediately following the command. In PowerShell read $LASTEXITCODE. In a POSIX shell read $?. Scripts can use the status to decide whether to proceed. The exit codes below describe blyxc itself.

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Command completed successfully. |
| 1 | Examples include a missing file, parser error or failed build. |
| 2 | Examples include an unknown command, a missing argument or an invalid run budget. |
| 4 | The interpreter reached a runtime failure, such as integer division by zero. |

#### Find the output file

With no -o option a native build puts the executable beside the source, using the platform executable extension. Pass an explicit output name when a project has several programs or when a script needs to invoke a known path.

#### Separate execution budgets

--max-steps controls a CLI interpreter run. The browser and the VS Code worker also enforce source, output and time limits. A native executable has ordinary process and system limits. These modes can differ for a very long or deeply recursive computation.

#### Practice

Choose the commands for a script that first checks the syntax of main.blyx, then runs it with a budget of 500 steps.

Hint

Check the exit status before starting the second command.

Solution

Use blyxc check main.blyx, followed on success by blyxc run main.blyx --max-steps 500. A parser success does not guarantee that execution will finish within the budget.

### [What Blyx 0.2.1 can run](https://doc.blyx-lang.space/guide/compatibility)

Choose an execution mode and identify features that are still being developed.

#### Choose an execution mode

Use the CLI interpreter or browser for immediate feedback. Use a native build to distribute a supported typed program to a compatible host. The editor and playground run the interpreter compiled to WebAssembly.

| Mode | Inputs and requirements | Limits to account for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser or desktop extension | A complete source buffer with fn main() | 256 KiB source, 64 KiB output and an eight-second worker deadline. |
| CLI interpreter | A .blyx file and the blyxc executable | Default one million evaluation steps and at most 64 simultaneous calls. |
| Native build | A supported typed program, rustc and a host linker | The generated program runs with system resources; interpreter step and call budgets do not apply. |

#### Supported execution

The teaching examples use functions, local bindings, scalar arithmetic, loops, recursion, numeric vectors and print macros. Native programs can import local .blyx modules and read command-line arguments or UTF-8 files through the host library. Use native-run or build for multi-file applications.

#### Features under development

The package registry and its dependency resolver are prototypes. The published source libraries use versioned Git checkouts. The browser and CLI interpreter execute a single source buffer. GPU kernels, a general tensor runtime, asynchronous tasks and actor scheduling remain development work.

#### Interpret a benchmark

Measure the same workload, input size and output across the implementations you compare. Separate startup costs from computational work when they answer different questions. The project’s published Fibonacci benchmark includes startup and reports its machine, raw samples and methodology.

#### Practice

Decide how to deliver a small numeric utility to a colleague who has no compiler installed. What do you need on each machine?

Hint

Distinguish the machine doing the build from the machine running the result.

Solution

On a suitable build host use blyxc, rustc and a linker to build the typed source. Deliver the executable for your colleague’s compatible OS and architecture. Try a small known input on the destination machine.
